translate.output: The various celestial bodies in the sky are called stars. Mercury is the Chen star. Venus is the Taibai star. When seen in the west at night, it is called Changgeng; when seen in the east in the morning, it is called Qiming. The Earth is also a planet. Mars is Yinghuo. Jupiter is the Suixing star. translate.gold: The heavenly bodies of the sky are called 星 "stars". Mercury is Chenxing. Venus is Taibai. When it appears in the west at night it is called Changgeng; when it appears in the east in the morning it is called Qiming. The earth, too, is a planet. Mars is Yinghuo. Jupiter is Suixing. Saturn is Zhenxing.

translate.output: That which is supreme and without equal is called Heaven. Heaven is the accumulation of qi. When it is still, it is called qi; when it moves, it is called wind. Those that move are planets; those that do not move are fixed stars. Fixed stars have light, while planets have none.
translate.gold: What is highest, with nothing above it, is called 天 "heaven". Heaven is accumulated air. When it is still it is called 氣 "air"; when it moves it is called 風 "wind". Those that move are planets; those that do not move are fixed stars. Fixed stars have light of their own; planets have none.

translate.output: My fifth maternal uncle saw me as far as Changsha; shaking my hand, he said, 'Next year I will send your wife to Beijing.' I replied, 'Beijing is a hardship; Uncle, please do not come.' He said, 'True. But in the end, I will seek out the place of your posting.' Having said this, he wept. I was unable to see my younger brother, so I entrusted Old Man Huang of Nan to tell him everything in person, hoping my brother would not let his emotions be stirred. He urged me again and again.
translate.gold: Fifth Uncle Nan saw me off as far as Changsha. Taking my hand, he said: "Next year I will bring your wife to the capital." I said: "Life in the capital is hard. Uncle, do not come." My uncle said: "Very well. But in the end I shall seek you out at your post." When he had finished speaking, he wept. I cannot see you, so I have asked Mr Huang Nan to tell you everything in person. I hope that you will not lose your temper. I urge this most earnestly, most earnestly.

translate.output: Copying the 'Thousand Character Classic' for calligraphy practice is acceptable, but one must be persevering. If you copy one hundred characters from a model every day without the slightest interruption, you will certainly become a calligrapher in a few years. Even when extremely busy, you must complete the day's lesson; do not make up for yesterday's delays today, nor do today's work in advance because you have matters to attend to tomorrow. Never interrupt your reading lessons because of family affairs, nor interrupt them because exams are approaching. Even on days when you are traveling, you may read upon arriving at a shop; on exam days, you may read after leaving the hall.
translate.gold: For practising calligraphy, copying the Thousand Character Classic is fine too, but you must persevere. Copy a hundred characters from the model every day, absolutely without a break, and in a few years you will certainly have become a calligrapher. Even when you are extremely busy, you must still finish each day's lessons on that day. Do not, because of a delay yesterday, make the work up today; and do not, because you will be busy tomorrow, do the work today in advance. On no account interrupt your daily reading because there is business at home, nor interrupt it because the examinations are approaching. Even on a travelling day you can read once you reach the inn; on an examination day you can read once you come out of the hall.
translate.judge_note: The translation uses 'shop' for 店, which is more accurately an inn or lodging.

Everything between heaven and earth changes without exception: day and night change to form a day; cold and heat change to form a year; ... if it were said that there is no change, then heaven, earth, and humanity would all cease to exist at once. translate.output: In that case, can the meaning of liberty actually not be implemented for the individual? [I respond]: What is this talk? The liberty of a group is the accumulation of individual liberties. A person cannot survive independently apart from a group; if a group does not preserve its liberty, then there will be other groups that invade, oppress, and seize it from the outside—in that case, what liberty could the individual possibly have? A person of shallow learning such as I, wishing to clarify this with a few meager words, how could I know if it is possible? ... Are there those in the world who love liberty? Let them be careful not to poison liberty, thereby poisoning the world.
translate.gold: In that case, can freedom after all not be applied to the individual? I answer: nonsense, what talk is this? Collective freedom is the sum of individual freedoms. People cannot survive on their own apart from the group. If the group does not protect its freedom, then other groups will come from outside to invade it, oppress it and plunder it, and then what will be left of the individual's freedom? For one of shallow learning like me to try to explain it in a few paltry words: how can I know that it will do? … Are there people in the world who love freedom? Let them take care not to poison freedom, and thereby poison the world.

translate.output: On the twenty-third day of the fourth month of the twenty-fourth year of Guangxu, the Cabinet received an imperial edict: For several years, officials both Chinese and foreign have studied current affairs, and many have advocated for reform to strengthen the nation. Recently, several edicts have been issued—such as establishing special examinations, reducing the number of soldiers, reforming the military examination system, and establishing primary and secondary schools; all have been repeatedly reviewed and thoroughly planned, and have just been proposed for implementation. However, this spirit has not yet widely prevailed, and arguments remain conflicted. Some, claiming to be experienced patriots, believe that old regulations must be strictly adhered to and new laws must be rejected; their clamorous talk is empty and provides no help. I ask: given the current state of affairs and the national situation, if we still rely on untrained soldiers, limited funds, scholars without practical learning, and craftsmen without skilled teachers—where strength and weakness are contrasted and the gap between rich and poor is vast—can we truly use a wooden club to strike against hardened armor and sharp weapons? ... The Imperial University of Peking should serve as a model for the various provinces and should especially be established first; the Grand Councilors and the Ministers of the Zongli Yamen are directed to jointly deliberate and submit a memorial with due haste. ... This is to be circulated and notified to all. By imperial command.
translate.gold: On the 23rd day of the 4th month of the 24th year of Guangxu, the Grand Secretariat received the following edict: For several years now, officials at court and in the provinces have studied current affairs, and most have advocated reform and self-strengthening. Recently edicts have been issued one after another: setting up a special examination, cutting surplus troops, reforming the military examinations, establishing schools of all levels. All were examined again and again and planned most thoroughly, and it has only just been proposed to put them into effect. But attitudes are not yet open, and opinions cannot agree. Some take cover behind experience and concern for the country, holding that the old institutions must be held fast and the new methods rejected. Many mouths clamour, but empty words are of no help. Let us ask: with the situation as it is today, and the state's strength as it is, if we still rely on untrained troops and limited funds, with scholars lacking practical learning and artisans lacking good teachers, the strong and the weak set side by side, the rich and the poor so far apart, can we really make clubs to beat strong armour and sharp weapons? … The Imperial University in the capital is to be an example to the provinces and above all should be set up first. Let the Grand Councillors and the princes and ministers of the Zongli Yamen deliberate on it jointly and report properly and quickly by memorial. … Let this be proclaimed to all. Respect this.
translate.judge_note: The translation incorrectly renders 衆喙嘵嘵,空言無補 as 'their clamorous talk is empty and provides no help,' when the reference translation's 'Many mouths clamour, but empty words are of no help' more accurately conveys the sense of pointless, repetitive criticism.

punctuate.output: 內務總長程德全，為呈報事。竊維保民衛國，警務實為行政之樞機；選賢任能，學校尤為儲才之淵藪。查南京現為首善之區，一應警察事宜，必先切實改良，方足為各省所表率。惟本部成立伊始，經費困難，凡屬布施，似宜力求撙節。爰將原有之江南高等巡警學堂，改為內務部警務學校。先招敎練所學警二百四十人，分科敎授為急，則治標之計；至正班學生，一俟籌有的欵，再行招考敎養，以副大總統謀進人民幸福之本意。並卽委任本部警務局長孫潤宇，兼任警務學校校長，以期迅速舉辦，庶於公私兩有裨益。所有開辦警務學校緣由，理應具文呈請鑒核施行。須至呈者：據稟邵伯湖西岸地土久荒，該代表等不忍棄利於地，籌辦墾殖誠不可緩。惟該岸共有地積若干，應計畆繪圖，先行呈部，以便飭交揚州民政長確查。仰該代表等迅卽遵照，並妥立招股章程辦法，一同呈部。此批。

translate.output: Cheng Dequan, Minister of Internal Affairs, submits this report. I humbly believe that for protecting the people and defending the nation, police affairs are truly the pivot of administration; for selecting the virtuous and appointing the capable, schools are especially the reservoirs of talent. It is found that Nanjing is currently the primary district of the capital; all police matters must first be practically improved before it can sufficiently serve as a model for the various provinces. However, since the inception of this Ministry, funding has been difficult. Regarding all expenditures, it seems appropriate to strive for frugality. Therefore, the existing Jiangnan Higher Police School is converted into the Ministry of Internal Affairs Police School. First, 200 and 40 students from the training centers will be recruited for specialized instruction, as an urgent measure to treat the symptoms. As for the regular students, once funds are secured, recruitment and education will be carried out to fulfill the President's original intention of advancing the happiness of the people. Furthermore, Sun Runyu, Director of the Ministry's Police Bureau, is concurrently appointed Principal of the Police School to ensure rapid organization, so that there may be benefit to both the public and private sectors. The reasons for establishing the Police School should properly be submitted in writing for your review and implementation. This is the reason for this submission. Regarding the report that the land on the west bank of Lake Shao has long been wasteland, and the representatives cannot bear to let the land's utility go to waste and are arranging for reclamation, this truly cannot be delayed. However, since there is a certain total area of land on that bank, the acreage should be calculated and a map drawn, then submitted to the Ministry first, so that the Civil Affairs Chief of Yangzhou may be ordered to verify it. The representatives are directed to comply immediately and to properly establish regulations for recruiting shareholders, to be submitted to the Ministry together. This is the reply.
translate.gold: Cheng Dequan, Minister of the Interior, reports as follows. I humbly consider that for protecting the people and defending the state, police affairs are the key to administration; and for choosing the worthy and employing the able, schools are the place where talent is gathered. I note that Nanjing is now the capital, and all police matters must first be thoroughly reformed before it can serve as a model for the provinces. But this ministry has only just been founded and funds are difficult, so all measures should, it seems, be as economical as possible. I have therefore converted the existing Jiangnan Higher Police School into the Ministry of the Interior Police School. It will first recruit 240 police cadets for the training institute and teach them by subject, as an emergency measure. As for students of the regular course, as soon as definite funds have been raised, they will be admitted by examination and educated, so as to fulfil the President's intention of working to advance the people's happiness. I have also at once appointed Sun Runyu, head of this ministry's police bureau, as principal of the police school concurrently, in the hope of setting it up quickly, so that both public and private interests may benefit. As to the opening of the police school, it is proper to prepare this document and request you to examine it and put it into effect. This petition is necessary. According to your petition, the land on the west shore of Lake Shaobo has long lain waste, and you representatives cannot bear to leave its profit in the ground and plan to reclaim and cultivate it. This truly cannot be delayed. But you should measure in mu how much land there is on that shore, draw a map and first submit them to the ministry, so that we can pass them on with an order to the civil governor of Yangzhou to verify. You representatives are directed to comply at once, and also to draw up proper regulations and procedures for raising capital, and submit them to the ministry together. This is the ruling.
translate.judge_note: The translation incorrectly renders '敎練所學警' as 'students from the training centers,' when it refers to police cadets undergoing training.

punctuate.output: 第一款，前壬寅年七月二十四日江寧所定和約，仍留照行。廣東所定善後舊約並通商章程，現在更章既經併入新約，所有舊約作為廢紙。第五十款，嗣後英國文書俱用英字書寫，暫時仍以漢文配送。俟中國選派學生學習英文，英語熟習，即不用配送漢文。自今以後，遇有文詞辯論之處，總以英文作為正義。此次定約，漢英文書詳細較對無訛，亦照此例。第五十一款，嗣後各式公文，無論京外內敘，大英國官民自不得提書「夷」字。
punctuate.gold: 第一款：前壬寅年七月二十四日江寧所定和約仍留照行。廣東所定善後舊約並通商章程現在更章，既經併入新約，所有舊約作為廢紙。第五十款：嗣後英國文書俱用英字書寫，暫時仍以漢文配送，俟中國選派學生學習英文、英語熟習，即不用配送漢文。自今以後，遇有文詞辯論之處，總以英文作為正義。此次定約，漢、英文書詳細較對無訛，亦照此例。第五十一款：嗣後各式公文，無論京外，內敘大英國官民，自不得提書夷字。

translate.output: Article 1: The peace treaty concluded at Jiangning on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month of the previous Renyin year shall continue to be observed as before. The old agreements for the settlement of affairs and the trade regulations concluded at Guangdong are now being revised; since they have been incorporated into the new treaty, all old agreements are to be treated as waste paper. Article 50: Henceforth, all British documents shall be written in English; for the time being, they will still be accompanied by a Chinese translation, but once China selects and sends students to study English and their proficiency becomes fluent, Chinese translations will no longer be required. From now on, wherever there is a dispute over the wording, the English text shall be taken as the authoritative version. In the conclusion of this treaty, the Chinese and English texts have been compared in detail and found to be without error, and shall follow this precedent. Article 51: Henceforth, in all types of official documents, whether inside or outside the capital, when referring to the officials or citizens of Great Britain, the term 'barbarian' (yi) must not be used.
translate.gold: Article 1: The peace treaty concluded earlier at Jiangning on the 24th day of the 7th month of the renyin year remains in force. The supplementary treaty concluded in Guangdong and the trade regulations are now revised; since they have been incorporated into the new treaty, all the old treaties are null and void. Article 50: From now on, British communications shall all be written in English. For the time being they will still be accompanied by Chinese; as soon as China has selected and sent students to learn English and they are proficient in the language, Chinese will no longer be sent with them. From now on, whenever there is a dispute about wording, the English shall in all cases be taken as the correct meaning. The treaty now concluded, of which the Chinese and English texts have been carefully checked and found without error, is also subject to this rule. Article 51: From now on, in official documents of all kinds, whether in the capital or the provinces, the character 夷 may not, of course, be written in referring to British officials and subjects.
translate.judge_note: The translation renders 夷 as 'barbarian,' which is a possible but overly literal and potentially loaded interpretation; a more neutral term like 'foreign' would be more accurate in conveying the intended meaning.

punctuate.output: 赫胥黎獨處一室之中，在英倫之南，背山而面野。檻外諸境歷歷如在几下。乃懸想二千年前，當羅馬大將愷徹未到時，此間有何景物？故知不變一言，決非天運，而悠久成物之理，轉在變動不居之中。是當前之所見，經廿年卅年而革，焉可也；更二萬年三萬年而革，亦可也。特據前事推將來，為變方長，未知所極而已。雖然，天運變矣，而有不變者行乎其中。不變惟何？是名「天演」。以天演為體，而其用有二：曰「物競」，曰「天擇」。此萬物莫不然而，於有生之類為尤著。物競者，物爭自存也。以一物以與物物爭，或存或亡，而其效則歸於天擇。天擇者，物爭焉而獨存，則其存也必有其所以存，必其所得於天之分，自致一己之能，與其所遭值之時與地，及凡周身以外之物力，有其相謀相劑者焉，夫而後獨免於亡，而足以自立也。而自其效觀之，若是物特為天之所厚而擇焉以存也者，夫是之謂天擇。天擇者，擇於自然，雖擇而莫之擇，猶物競之無所爭，而實天下之至爭也。斯賓塞爾曰：「天擇者，存其最宜者也。」夫物既爭存矣，而天又從其爭之後而擇之。一爭一擇，而變化之事出矣。

translate.output: Huxley sat alone in a room in the south of England, with mountains at his back and the wild before him; the various scenes outside his window were as clear as if they were right beneath his desk. He then imagined what the scenery here must have been two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Caesar arrived. ... Thus, we know that the claim that nothing changes is certainly not the way of heaven. On the contrary, the principle by which enduring things are formed lies precisely within constant change. Therefore, what we see before us may be transformed in twenty or thirty years, and it may also be transformed in twenty or thirty thousand years. Simply extrapolating the future from past events, the process of change is long, and its limit is unknown. Nevertheless, while the way of heaven changes, there is something unchanging that operates within it. What is this unchanging thing? It is called 'Celestial Evolution.' Celestial Evolution is the substance, and its functions are twofold: 'struggle for existence' and 'natural selection.' Nothing in the universe is exempt from this, and it is especially prominent among living beings. 'Struggle for existence' means that things compete to survive. When one thing competes with others, it may survive or perish, and the result is determined by natural selection. 'Natural selection' means that among those that struggle, one alone survives. If it survives, it must have a reason for surviving: it must have a portion granted by heaven, the development of its own abilities, the timing and location it encountered, and the external resources surrounding it, all working together in harmony. Only then does it escape perishability and become sufficient to stand on its own. Viewing it from the result, if a thing is specially favored and selected by heaven to survive, this is called natural selection. Natural selection is a selection made by nature; although it is a selection, there is no selector, just as in the struggle for existence there is no specific opponent, yet it is in fact the ultimate competition in the world. Spencer said: 'Natural selection is the preservation of the most fit.' Once things have struggled to survive, heaven selects from among them after the struggle; through one struggle and one selection, the process of evolution emerges.
translate.gold: Huxley is sitting alone in a room in the south of England, with hills behind and fields in front; the scenes beyond the railing are as clear as if they lay below his desk. He then imagines what this place looked like two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Caesar came. …… Hence we know that "unchanging" is by no means the way of heaven's course, and that the principle by which things endure and take shape lies, on the contrary, in ceaseless change. What we see before us may well be transformed in twenty or thirty years, or again in twenty or thirty thousand. It is only that, inferring the future from past events, change has far still to run, and we do not know where it will end. And yet, though heaven's course changes, something unchanging operates within it. What is this unchanging thing? It is called evolution (天演). Evolution is the substance, and it has two functions: the struggle of things (物競) and the selection of heaven (天擇). This is so of all things, and most evident among living things. The struggle of things is things striving to preserve themselves. When one thing contends with thing after thing, it either survives or perishes, and the result comes down to the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is when things contend and one alone survives. Then there must be a reason for its survival: its endowment from heaven, the abilities it attains by itself, the time and place it meets with, and all the forces of things outside its body must have worked together and complemented one another. Only then does it alone escape perishing and become able to stand on its own. And looking at it from the result, it is as if this thing had been specially favoured by heaven and selected to survive: this is what is called the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is selection by nature: it selects, yet no one selects; just as the struggle of things seems to be no struggle, and is in truth the fiercest struggle in the world. Spencer said: "The selection of heaven is the preservation of the fittest." Since things struggle to survive, and heaven then selects among them after their struggle, with each struggle and each selection, change comes about.
translate.judge_note: The translation's rendering of 檻外諸境 as 'the various scenes outside his window' loses the sense of a formal, enclosed garden or estate, which is implied by the original.

punctuate.output: 中國政治與文化之變革，莫劇於殷周之際。殷周間之大變革，自其表言之，不過一姓一家之興亡與都邑之移轉；自其裏言之，則舊制度廢而新制度興，舊文化廢而新文化興。又自其表言之，則古聖人之所以取天下及所以守之者，若無以異於後世之帝王；而自其裏言之，則其制度文物與其立制之本意，乃出於萬世治安之大計，其心術與規摹，迥非後世帝王所能夢見也。欲觀周之所以定天下，必自其制度始矣。周人制度之大異於商者：一曰立子立嫡之制，由是而生宗法及喪服之制，並由是而有封建子弟之制，君天子、臣諸侯之制；二曰廟數之制；三曰同姓不婚之制。此數者，皆周之所以綱紀天下，其旨則在納上下於道德，而合天子、諸侯、卿大夫、士、庶民，以成一道德之團體。周公制作之本意，實在於此，此非穿鑿附會之言也。茲篇所論，皆有事實爲之根據，試略述之。其條例則《春秋左氏傳》之說曰：「太子死，有母弟則立之，無則立長，年鈞擇賢，義鈞則卜。」公羊家之說曰：「禮，嫡夫人無子，立右媵；右媵無子，立左媵。」此二說中，後說尤爲詳密，顧皆後儒充類之說，當立法之初，未必窮其變至此。然所謂「立子以貴不以長，立適以長不以賢」者，乃傳子法之精髓，當時雖未必有此語，固已用此意矣。

translate.output: Of the transformations in China's politics and culture, none were more dramatic than those between the Yin and Zhou dynasties. ... The great transformation between the Yin and Zhou, speaking of its surface, was nothing more than the rise and fall of one surname and family and the relocation of the capital; speaking of its interior, however, the old system was abolished and a new system arose, and the old culture was abolished and a new culture arose. Again, speaking of its surface, the means by which the ancient sages won the world and the means by which they maintained it seem no different from those of later emperors; but speaking of its interior, their systems, cultural artifacts, and the original intent behind establishing those systems emerged from a grand plan for the peace and order of ten thousand generations; their mental methods and blueprints were vastly different from what later emperors could have dreamed of. To observe how the Zhou settled the world, one must begin with their system. The ways in which the Zhou system differed greatly from that of the Shang were: first, the system of establishing the heir and the legitimate line, from which the system of lineage (zongfa) and mourning garments arose, and from which also came the system of enfeoffing sons and younger brothers, and the system of the Son of Heaven as sovereign and the feudal lords as ministers; second, the system regarding the number of ancestral temples; third, the system prohibiting marriage between those of the same surname. These few points were all the means by which the Zhou organized the world. Their purpose lay in bringing those above and below under the fold of morality, uniting the Son of Heaven, feudal lords, high officials, great officers, scholars, and commoners into a single moral community. The original intent of the Duke of Zhou's system-making truly lay here. These are not words of forced interpretation or contrived association; the arguments in this essay are all based on facts, which I shall attempt to describe briefly. ... As for the regulations, the view in the 'Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals' says: 'If the crown prince dies and there is a younger brother of the same mother, establish him; if not, establish the eldest. If ages are equal, choose the virtuous; if virtue is equal, cast lots.' The Gongyang school says: 'According to ritual, if the primary wife has no son, establish the son of the right concubine; if the right concubine has no son, establish the son of the left concubine...' Of these two views, the latter is especially detailed, yet both are theories expanded upon by later Confucian scholars; at the beginning of the legislation, it is unlikely they had exhausted all variations to this extent. However, the saying 'establish a son based on nobility, not seniority; establish a successor based on seniority, not virtue' is the essence of the law of succession; although such words may not have existed at the time, this intent was certainly employed.
translate.gold: Of all the changes in China's government and culture, none is more drastic than that at the transition from Shang to Zhou. …… The great change between Shang and Zhou, seen from the surface, was no more than the rise and fall of one family and the moving of the capital; seen from within, old institutions fell and new institutions arose, old culture fell and new culture arose. Again, seen from the surface, the ways in which the ancient sages won the empire and kept it seem no different from those of later emperors; but seen from within, their institutions, their culture and their original intention in founding the institutions came in fact from a grand plan for order and peace for ten thousand generations, and their thinking and design were far beyond anything later emperors could dream of. If one wishes to see how the Zhou settled the empire, one must begin from its institutions. The Zhou institutions that differ greatly from the Shang are, first, the institution of succession by the son and by the son of the principal wife, from which arose the lineage system and the mourning system, and from which came the enfeoffment of sons and younger brothers and the system in which the Son of Heaven is lord and the feudal lords are subjects; second, the number of ancestral temples; third, the rule that those of the same surname do not marry. These are all the means by which the Zhou gave order to the empire. Their purpose was to bring high and low within morality, and to unite the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, ministers, great officers, gentlemen and the common people into one moral community. The Duke of Zhou's original intention in making institutions truly lay here. These are not far-fetched or forced words: everything this essay argues has facts as its evidence. Let me set it out briefly. …… The rules are given in the account of the *Zuo Commentary*: "When the heir dies, if there is a younger brother by the same mother, he is made heir; if not, the eldest is made heir. If they are equal in age, the worthiest is chosen; if equal in merit, the matter is divined." The Gongyang school's account says: "By the rites, if the principal wife has no son, the son of the right secondary wife is made heir; if the right secondary wife has no son, the son of the left secondary wife is made heir; ……" Of these two accounts, the latter is especially detailed, but both are the extrapolations of later Confucians; when the rule was first laid down, its makers did not necessarily work out every case in this way. Yet what is called "a son is made heir by rank, not by age; the son of the principal wife is made heir by age, not by worth" is the essence of the rule of succession by sons; though these words may not have been said at the time, the idea was certainly already in use.
translate.judge_note: The translation misses the nuance that the 'interior' perspective on the Shang-Zhou transition involves a deeper understanding of the underlying principles and motivations, rather than simply stating that 'old institutions fell and new institutions arose'.

punctuate.output: 弟向獲締交於季方，因得聞元方之賢，思一見爲快。昨於會城邂逅遇之，覺大兄之才華器宇更有勝於所聞者。正恨相見之晚，不期越宿分襟；又恨相違之速矣。別後初四日抵津門，初十日詣平舒。月未一圓，地經兩易，風塵僕僕，無非芸人之田，自憐亦堪自笑。比值同人歸里，館中惟我獨居，加以清磬紅魚，直是修行古剎；而西風黃葉，洄溯時殷。雙鯉之頒，定不我棄。尊體復元否？嫁務紛勞，諸宜珍攝。因風寄意，不盡所懷。久不見碧梧翠竹之姿，每於月白風清，輒深神往。且以足下久不入直爲疑，近得阮昔侯札，知駕遊山左，種蓮楚邱者已非一日。青萍結綠，到處爭售，所固然也。令弟才華意氣滿，謂「嵆山獨鶴，足以振采雞羣」，何期牙琴一摧，墓草已宿，令人感慨係之。弟初客遼西，旋遊津淀，今春復有平舒之役。年年壓線依舊，幫傭良由，村女蛾眉難爲時賞耳。

translate.output: I previously formed a close friendship with Jifang, and through him I heard of Yuanfang's virtue and longed for the pleasure of meeting you. Yesterday, I happened upon you in Huicheng, and I felt that your talent and bearing were even greater than what I had heard. I just regretted that we met so late, and unexpectedly, having spent only one night together, we had to part; I now regret the speed of our separation. After parting, I arrived at Tianjin on the fourth, and reached Pingshu on the tenth; before the moon had completed its cycle, I had changed locations twice. Traveling in dust and toil is nothing more than the lot of a wandering scholar; I pity myself, yet it is also laughable. Recently, my colleagues returned to their hometowns, leaving me alone in the guest house; with the sound of the clear chime and the sight of red fish, it is truly like an ancient Buddhist temple. As the west wind blows the yellow leaves and the river traffic is busy, I trust that your letter will not abandon me. Has your health recovered? The affairs of marriage are exhausting, so please take good care of yourself. I send my thoughts by this breeze, though I cannot express all that is in my heart. I have long missed the sight of your elegant presence; whenever the moon is bright and the breeze is clear, I am deeply longing for you. Moreover, I wondered why you had not reported for duty for so long. Recently I received a letter from Ruan Xihou and learned that you have been traveling in the south, planting lotuses in Chuqiu for some time. That the green duckweed has flourished and is being sold everywhere is only natural. My younger brother, with his talent and spirit, fully believed that you were like a solitary crane of Mount Jishan, capable of outshining the crowd; who could have expected that the ivory zither would be broken and the grave-grass would grow old, leaving one filled with emotion! I first stayed as a guest in Liaoxi, then traveled to the Tianjin estuary. This spring, I have again been assigned to a post in Pingshu. Year after year I am pushed to the frontier, still working as a hired hand; this is truly because the beauty of a village girl is difficult to appreciate in these times.
translate.gold: I, your younger brother, formerly had the good fortune to make friends with your younger brother, and so heard of your worth as the elder, and longed for the pleasure of meeting you. Yesterday I met you by chance in the provincial capital, and felt that your talent and bearing surpassed even what I had heard. Just as I was regretting that we had not met sooner, we unexpectedly parted after a single night, and now I regret that we were separated so soon. After we parted, I reached Tianjin on the fourth and went to Pingshu on the tenth: in less than a month I have changed place twice. Travel-worn, I do nothing but weed other people's fields; I pity myself, and can also laugh at myself. Just now my colleagues have gone home, and I live alone in the office; add the clear chime and the red wooden fish, and it is just like an old temple for religious practice. With the west wind and the yellow leaves, I often long for you deeply; you will surely not abandon me, but will send me a letter. Have you recovered your health? With the wedding arrangements so many and tiring, please take good care of yourself. I send my thoughts by the wind, and cannot express all I feel. I have long not seen your bearing, like green parasol trees and jade bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the wind clear, I long for you in spirit. I had wondered why you had not been on duty for so long. Recently I received a letter from Ruan Xihou and learnt that you have travelled to Shandong and have long been serving in a secretariat at Chuqiu. Fine swords and fine jade are sought after everywhere: that is only to be expected. Your younger brother's talent and spirit, I was sure, like Ji Shao, the lone crane, would shine among the flock of chickens. Who could have expected that Boya's zither would be broken, and that the grass on the grave is already a year old? It moves one to sorrow! I, your younger brother, first lived in Liaoxi, then soon moved to Tianjin and its lakes. This spring I have again taken up a post at Pingshu. Year after year I sew for others, still a hired hand: truly because a village girl's fine eyebrows are hard for the age to admire.
translate.judge_note: The translation misses the nuance that the speaker is lamenting the brevity of their encounter, stating they 'unexpectedly parted after a single night' rather than regretting they met late.
